summaries.example: Imagine a classroom garden. The teacher helps the plants grow, but the plants, sunlight, water, and students' choices all matter too. In process theism, God is like the greatest helper and guide, not the only source of every change. God also knows and cares about what happens, including joy and suffering.
summaries.summary: Process theism is a way of thinking about God that begins with change, time, and relationships. It is linked especially with Whitehead and Hartshorne. Traditional theism often describes God as outside time, unchanging, and untouched by the world. Process theism instead says that God is everlasting in some ways but also experiences the world's events and responds to them. God is the greatest creative power, yet creatures have smaller creative powers of their own. This means the world is made through cooperation, rather than by God's one-sided control alone. Process thinkers also describe the future as partly open. God knows what has happened and what is happening, while some future possibilities have not yet been settled. Whitehead and Hartshorne develop different accounts of how God's lasting identity and changing experience fit together. Their ideas are philosophical proposals, so they are discussed and tested through reasoning rather than simply accepted as revealed answers.
key_ideas: Process theism was especially shaped by Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne.
God and the world are in a two-way relationship: God affects the world, and the world affects God's experience.
God is very powerful, but creatures also have some real freedom and creative power.
The future is not completely finished, so God knows the past and present fully while some future events remain open.
Process thinkers say love includes caring about another's feelings, not merely deciding what is good for that person.
summaries.why_it_matters: This view changes how people think about power, freedom, love, suffering, and the future. It offers one response to the problem of evil: perhaps God does not control every event, because creatures and other parts of nature have genuine power of their own. It also presents God as a caring companion who is affected by the world's joys and sorrows. Whether this picture works better than other views is a matter for philosophical debate.

important_terms.definition: The idea that reality is always becoming and changing, and that things exist through their relationships with other things.
A family of ideas saying that God is involved in time, affected by the world, and related to the world's ongoing changes.
The power of things to make something new happen. Process thinkers say creatures have some of this power, as well as God.
The view that the world is in God but is not exactly the same as God.

questions_to_think_about: Would a loving God need to be able to feel something about what happens to creatures?
Can people be genuinely free if every choice has already been decided?
Is a world with real chances for good and harm better than a world with no real choices?
What might it mean for the world to be in God without being identical to God?

summaries.example: Consider a group designing a community park. A city authority may establish rules and suggest a plan, but residents, workers, weather, and living things all contribute to what the park becomes. The result is not simply imposed by one agent. Process theism uses a larger version of this idea: God supplies possibilities, order, and value, while finite beings make real contributions and can resist one another. The analogy is limited, because process thinkers still hold that God's existence is not dependent on any particular creature or universe.
summaries.summary: Process theism is a philosophical family associated chiefly with Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne. Its central proposal is that God is not wholly outside temporal becoming. God is everlasting and unsurpassed in certain respects, but God also receives the world's actual events, responds to them, and is affected by them. This opposes the classical model in which God is entirely immutable and impassible, although process theists do not reject every form of permanence or necessity. The disagreement begins with creativity. Classical theism commonly reserves creation in the strict sense for God alone, whereas process metaphysics treats every actual entity as possessing some degree of self-determining creative power. God is therefore the eminent creative power among many lesser creators. The world is not dependent on God for its existence in exactly the same way that God depends on the world's particular events: God's existence is not precarious, but the world's history changes God's experience and achieved value. Whitehead explains this through God's primordial and consequent natures. Hartshorne develops a different model, distinguishing necessary divine existence and essence from contingent divine actuality. Both models support a reciprocal, or panentheistic, relation in which the world is in God without being identical with God. These ideas also reshape debates about evil, freedom, omnipotence, and future knowledge. Process theists argue that genuine freedom requires real alternatives and that persuasion is a more fitting form of divine power than total coercive control. They also hold that an unsettled future is not an object waiting to be fully known as settled fact.
key_ideas: Process theism challenges the classical picture of God as wholly timeless, immutable, impassible, and unaffected by the world, while retaining some forms of divine permanence.
Whitehead and Hartshorne treat creativity as universal: God is the supreme creative power, but finite entities are co-creators rather than merely passive products.
The God-world relation is reciprocal. Divine activity provides possibilities, aims, and order; worldly activity contributes new actuality and value to divine experience.
Whitehead analyzes God's duality through primordial and consequent natures. Hartshorne instead emphasizes the distinction between necessary divine existence and changing divine actuality.
Process theism interprets omnipotence as persuasion rather than unilateral coercion. No agent can simply determine another free actual entity's decision.
Because the future is partly unsettled, divine knowledge includes the determinate past, the present process of becoming, and the future's still-open possibilities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Process theism offers a systematic alternative to both classical theism and atheistic interpretations of change. Its account of divine relativity aims to make compassion, creaturely freedom, and the world's real value philosophically intelligible. It also reframes the problem of evil: if finite beings possess genuine creative power, not every harmful event can be attributed to a unilateral divine decision. At the same time, the view faces serious questions about divine power, omniscience, the coherence of its metaphysics, and whether a changing God can still be necessary or perfect.

important_terms.definition: A metaphysical approach that treats becoming, temporal development, and relations among entities as basic features of reality.
A family of philosophical theologies influenced by Whitehead and Hartshorne, holding that God is essentially related to and affected by temporal processes.
The metaphysical principle that every actual entity has some capacity both to affect others and to respond to what affects it.
The claim that relations from creatures to God are real because creaturely events alter God's experience, not merely human descriptions of God.
Whitehead's name for God's awareness of possibilities, contrasted with the consequent nature, which receives the world's actual history.
Hartshorne's distinction between God's necessary existence and character, and the contingent, changing states in which God experiences the world.

questions_to_think_about: Does a God who is affected by the world have a more coherent account of compassion than a wholly impassible God?
Can divine power remain supreme if it cannot unilaterally determine every creaturely decision?
Does an open future limit omniscience, or does it accurately describe what there is to know?
Which account better preserves divine identity: Whitehead's single actual entity with two natures, or Hartshorne's enduring individual with successive actual states?
Can the process account of creativity explain evil without making God responsible for every harmful decision?

summaries.example: Think about a soccer team planning a play. A coach can suggest a strategy and encourage each player, but the players still make choices, opponents react, and the final play can turn out differently from the plan. Process theism compares God's action more to guiding and persuading than to controlling every movement. The world contributes to what happens, and God responds to that contribution.
summaries.summary: Process theism is a group of ideas about God influenced especially by Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne. It begins with a picture of reality as an ongoing process: things come into being, change, respond to one another, and contribute to what happens next. Traditional forms of theism often describe God as eternal in the sense of being outside time, unchanging, and unaffected by the world. Process theism argues instead that God is everlasting and supreme in some ways, but also participates in time and is genuinely affected by worldly events. A major disagreement concerns creativity. In classical theism, God alone is creator in the strictest sense. In process philosophy, every actual being has at least a small ability to determine its own activity. God is the greatest creative power, but creatures are lesser co-creators. This makes the God-world relationship two-sided: God offers possibilities, order, and guidance, while creatures add new experiences and achievements to God's life. Whitehead and Hartshorne explain this relationship differently. Whitehead speaks of two inseparable aspects of God: a primordial side concerned with possibilities and a consequent side that receives the world's actual history. Hartshorne distinguishes God's necessary existence and excellent character from the changing ways God actually experiences and knows the world. Process theism is often connected with panentheism, the view that the world is within God without exhausting or equaling God. These ideas affect debates about freedom, evil, love, divine power, and knowledge of the future. Process thinkers generally say that God persuades rather than totally coerces, and that the future contains genuine possibilities that have not yet become settled facts.
key_ideas: Whitehead and Hartshorne developed different versions of process theism, so their views should not be treated as identical.
Traditional theism often describes God as timeless and unaffected, while process theism says God is temporal and responsive in some respects.
Creatures have real but limited creative power, so the world is not produced by God's action alone.
God's relationship with the world helps explain why process thinkers describe God as caring about creaturely happiness and suffering.
Process theists usually say that the future is partly open, rather than already being a completely finished set of facts.
The theory is based on philosophical reflection and metaphysics, not on claiming that a private revelation settles every question.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because it offers a different way to connect divine goodness with a changing and sometimes painful world. It presents love as more than wishing good for others: love also involves sensitivity to their actual experiences. It gives creatures meaningful responsibility, since their decisions help shape reality. Critics and supporters continue to disagree about whether this account preserves enough divine power and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The view that change, growth, time, and relationships are basic parts of reality rather than minor details.
A type of philosophical theology saying that God is involved in the world's changing events and is affected by them.
The ability to contribute to what happens next. Process thinkers say both God and creatures have creative power, though not equally.
The idea that God's relationship with the world works in both directions: God affects creatures, and creatures affect God's experience.
The view that the world exists within God but is not simply identical to God.
A form of power that encourages or presents possibilities instead of forcing another being's decision.

questions_to_think_about: Is a God who can be affected by the world stronger or weaker than a God who cannot change?
Would complete control leave room for meaningful human freedom?
If God does not know an unsettled future as already settled, is that a limitation or accurate knowledge?
How might shared creative power change the usual explanation of suffering?
Does saying that everything is in God differ from saying that everything is God?
